justification: Contribution is a framework that dynamically adjusts group composition and studies emergent inter-agent behaviour; lab experiments show groups beating a single agent, no deployment.
Claim is tree-structured exploration of the solution space with backtracking via a ToT controller; evidence is a prototype Sudoku solver compared against the plain LLM in the lab.
Title-only record: multi-critic plan selection selects among candidate plans to suppress echo cascades; no abstract, so only a proposed mechanism is visible and no evaluation is evidenced.
Claim compares a nine-role multi-agent orchestration against a two-agent generator-reflector loop over a shared design-state graph; 60 lab runs across 2 LLMs x 2 configs x 3 temperatures x 5 seeds.
Theory of Mind module scaffolds hierarchical planning by generating and refining hypotheses that drive high-level action choice; validated in the lab on Melting Pot (runner-up critique_and_revision).
Contribution is a best-first tree search over environment states with explicit exploration at inference; lab results on VisualWebArena and WebArena, no real deployment.

ACE rewrites the agent's own context playbook from execution feedback across episodes (offline prompts, online memory); benchmark results on agent and finance suites (runner-up memory_and_context_management).
Contribution substitutes repeated LLM tool-selection calls with a cheap trajectory-derived transition graph, claiming up to 30% inference-cost cuts; lab experiments across agent tasks.
Outer loop fine-tunes the model on its own self-refined responses over successive self-evolution iterations; lab experiments on mathematics and general tasks without human intervention.
Object of study is a self-feedback mechanism where the LLM evaluates then refines its own queries and answers; measured on the BioASQ CLEF 2025 challenge data, a lab benchmark setting.
Self-Refine is the revise-on-own-feedback loop itself, one LLM as generator, feedback provider and refiner; validated in the lab across 7 established tasks against one-step generation.

Novelty is Structured Evidence Assessment, an analytical gating module that audits evidence for gaps and repeats until evidence is verified sufficient; lab results on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue.
Contribution is self-debugging: the model explains and repairs its own program from execution results with no human feedback; lab benchmark results on Spider, TransCoder and MBPP.
ProMiSe iteratively refines a response one quality principle at a time using external proxy-metric feedback; validated in the lab on MultiDoc2Dial and QuAC.

Paper's object is whether verbalized self-feedback refinement is worth its cost, proposing feedback-free retrials instead; lab comparison of refinement frameworks against the simpler retrial condition.

Multi-Aspect Feedback is an iterative refinement framework whose contribution is the per-error-category critique fed back for rewriting; lab gains reported on mathematical reasoning and logical entailment.
Contribution is the debate arrangement itself, several agents in tit-for-tat with a judge managing the process, proposed against single-agent reflection; lab results on two reasoning datasets.
SummIt refines a summary iteratively through self-evaluation and feedback, and reports overcorrection as a finding; automatic evaluation on three benchmark summarization datasets plus a human check.
Contribution is critique generation fed back to humans and to the model to refine summaries; evidence is lab studies where human evaluators using the critiques find flaws they otherwise missed.
CRITIC's claim is the verify-then-amend loop in which external tool feedback drives progressive revision; lab evaluations on free-form QA, mathematical program synthesis and toxicity reduction.
Empirical audit of intrinsic self-correction, showing reasoning performance degrades when a model revises without external feedback; lab experiments on reasoning tasks, not a deployed setting.
Agents improve each other across repeated negotiation rounds by self-play plus in-context learning from a critic's AI feedback; lab game with deal price as metric across models and roles.

TEaR is a translate-estimate-refine self-refinement loop whose claim is that self-feedback drives error reduction; lab evaluation with automatic metrics and MQM scores against internal and external feedback.
Studies why self-refinement fails, showing the self-refine pipeline amplifies self-bias; lab analysis of six LLMs on translation, constrained generation and mathematical reasoning datasets.
Contribution is the debate arrangement itself, several agents in tit-for-tat with a judge managing the process, proposed against single-agent reflection; lab results on two reasoning datasets.
